sec: HAV vs HEV prevention, serology graph and ALF classification

items.q: What is the incidence of fulminant hepatic failure in acute Hepatitis A versus acute Hepatitis E in pregnancy?
opts: HAV: rare (1 in 2 lakhs); HEV in pregnancy: approximately 20%
items.exp: Risk of fulminant failure is rare in HAV (1 in 2 lakhs), whereas in HEV it is 1–2% in general but reaches 20% in pregnancy. (Book p994)

items.q: What are the typical recovery durations for acute Hepatitis A versus acute Hepatitis E infections?
items.exp: The comparison table notes a recovery time of 8 weeks for HAV and 12 weeks for HEV. (Book p994)

items.q: Match each hepatitis virus with its specific medical therapy — 1) Hepatitis A fluid and glucose repletion 2) Hepatitis E with long-standing cholestasis … A) Oral or systemic steroids B) 150 mL of 10% Dextrose
items.exp: Conservative glucose repletion for HAV uses 150 mL 10% Dextrose, whereas long-standing cholestasis in HEV is treated with steroids. (Book p994)

items.q: Fill up: Acute relapsing hepatitis occurring > 6–12 months after the initial infection is observed in ______ but is absent in Hepatitis E.
items.exp: The table notes '+ (Relapse >6–12 months)' under HAV for acute relapsing hepatitis, while HEV has a dash. (Book p994)

items.q: What is the recommended dosing schedule and pre-exposure timing for the HAVRIX Hepatitis A vaccine?
opts: 1 mL IM, 2 doses given 6–12 months apart; pre-exposure >= 2 weeks before travel
0.5 mL SC, single dose; pre-exposure within 48 hours of travel
2 mL IM, 3 doses at 0, 1, 6 months; pre-exposure 6 weeks before travel
1 mL oral drops, 2 doses 4 weeks apart; pre-exposure 1 week before travel
items.exp: HAVRIX is given as 1 mL IM in 2 doses 6–12 months apart; pre-exposure prophylaxis is >= 2 weeks before travel, and post-exposure within 4 weeks. (Book p994)

items.q: Which three laboratory parameters constitute the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score noted on this page?
opts: INR, Serum Bilirubin, and Serum Creatinine
Albumin, Prothrombin time, and Ascites grade
ALT, Platelet count, and Serum Sodium
GGT, Alkaline phosphatase, and Encephalopathy grade
items.exp: The MELD score components are explicitly listed as INR, Serum Bilirubin, and Serum Creatinine. (Book p994)

items.q: A traveler returns from an endemic zone with acute viral hepatitis A. Serological plotting over the 20-week exposure window demonstrates stool virus shedding followed by jaundice. At what post-exposure time frame does fecal HAV shedding peak and drop, and which antibody provides lifelong immunity?
opts: Fecal shedding peaks before 4 weeks and drops by 6 weeks; IgG Anti-HAV provides lifelong immunity
Fecal shedding peaks at 12 weeks and drops at 20 weeks; IgM Anti-HAV provides lifelong immunity
Fecal shedding persists continuously for 12 months; IgA Anti-HAV provides lifelong immunity
Fecal shedding only begins after week 16; Anti-HBs provides lifelong immunity
items.exp: The graph shows fecal HAV peaking before week 4 and dropping by week 6; IgG Anti-HAV rises after weeks 8–12 conferring lifelong protection. (Book p994)

items.q: What is the clinical definition of Acute Liver Failure (ALF)?
opts: Acute hepatitis with encephalopathy (cerebral edema) and coagulopathy (INR >= 1.5) without pre-existing liver disease
Decompensation of established cirrhosis with ascites, variceal bleeding, and jaundice
Severe transaminitis >1000 U/L persisting for more than 6 months in a chronic carrier
Biliary tract obstruction complicated by ascending cholangitis and septic shock
items.exp: ALF is defined as acute hepatitis plus encephalopathy (cerebral edema) and coagulopathy (INR >= 1.5) in the absence of pre-existing liver disease. (Book p994)

items.q: Match each classification of acute liver failure with its onset interval from jaundice to encephalopathy — 1) Fulminant (Hyperacute) 2) Acute 3) Subacute … A) 7–21 days B) 21 days to 26 weeks C) < 7 days
items.exp: Onset intervals are Fulminant (Hyperacute): < 7 days; Acute: 7–21 days; and Subacute: 21 days to 26 weeks. (Book p994)

items.q: What is the most common cause of Acute Liver Failure in India?
items.exp: Under viral causes of ALF, HEV (1–2%) is explicitly tagged as '(m/c in India)'. (Book p994)

items.q: What is the risk of developing acute liver failure in patients with Hepatitis B and Hepatitis D virus coinfection?
items.exp: The risk of ALF in HBV + HDV coinfection is listed as 5–20% (compared to 0.1–1% for isolated HBV). (Book p994)

items.q: Assess the two statements: I Hepatitis E carries no commercial vaccine approved for routine clinical prevention. II Post-exposure prophylaxis for Hepatitis A using HAVRIX vaccine must be administered within 4 weeks of exposure.
items.exp: Both statements are true: HEV has 'No vaccine' listed, and HAVRIX post-exposure prophylaxis is given 'within 4 wks'. (Book p994)
